title: Throughput in the port of Rotterdam rose by 0.9% in the first nine months of the year
key_claim: Transhipment throughput fell by 20% in the first nine months of 2026 as long-standing capacity restraints at deep-sea terminals pushed cargo to other ports, while hinterland volume rose 7.2%.
frame_summary: Presents nine-month 2026 throughput as modest growth held up by hinterland flows, argues deep-sea terminal capacity limits are pushing cargo to other ports, and calls for investment in road, waterway and rail networks.
verbatim_quote: In contrast, transhipment throughput fell by 20%.
verbatim_list: Total throughput in the port of Rotterdam rose by 0.9% in the first nine months of 2026 compared to the same period last year. This brought the total throughput to 323.2 million tonnes.
Container throughput in TEU remained at a similar level to a year earlier, with a slight growth of 0.1% in the first nine months of 2026.
Measured in tonnes, throughput fell by 2.2%.
Due to long-standing capacity restraints at deep-sea terminals in Rotterdam, more cargo is being handled via other ports,
Hinterland volume rose by 7.2% in the last nine months.
This growth was chiefly the result of an 8.9% increase in the import of full containers.
notes: Primary port-authority release; the canonical statement that capacity, not demand, is moving cargo elsewhere.

title: Commission approves €286 million German State aid to port of Hamburg
date_evidence: 2026-11-13-eu-approves-286-million-german-state-aid-for-new-quays-in-port-of-hamburg (Lovguiden mirror of the Commission press corner item, published_time 2026-11-13, dateline 13 November 2026)
key_claim: The Commission approved two €143 million German measures for infrastructure works at the Salzgitter and Steinwerder quays in the port of Hamburg.
frame_summary: Approves €286 million of quay-renewal aid as compatible infrastructure support for the port of Hamburg under EU State aid rules.
verbatim_quote: The European Commission has approved, under EU State aid rules, two €143 million German measures to support infrastructure works in the port of Hamburg.
verbatim_list: The measures concern two distinct infrastructure projects, one at the Salzgitter quay and one at the Steinwerder quay.

title: Hamburger Hafen: Umschlagszahlen 1. bis 3. Quartal 2026 auf einen Blick
key_claim: The Port of Hamburg handled 84.5 million tonnes (down 2.6%) and 6.1 million TEU (down 2.8%) in the first three quarters of 2026, with strikes and extensive container-terminal modernisation among the named causes.
frame_summary: Presents the nine-month decline as stabilising after weather losses, oil-market disruption from the Iran war, strikes and container-terminal modernisation, arguing the modernisation will pay off in the long term.
verbatim_quote: In den ersten neun Monaten des Jahres wurden im Hamburger Hafen insgesamt 6,1 Mio. TEU umgeschlagen,
verbatim_list: Der Gesamtumschlag lag in Deutschlands größtem Seehafen in den ersten neun Monaten des Jahres 84,5 Mio. Tonnen.
(gegenüber dem gleichen Zeitraum im Vorjahr: -2,8 Prozent TEU bzw. -2,6 Prozent Tonnen)
Maßgeblich für die gegenüber dem Vorjahreszeitraum leicht schwächere Entwicklung (-2,6 Prozent) waren witterungsbedingte Einbußen zu Beginn des Jahres,
Hinzu kamen umfangreiche Containerterminal-Modernisierungsmaßnahmen,
und zuletzt auch Streiks, die sich auf den Gesamtumschlag der drei Quartale auswirken.
notes: German original of the port's official nine-month figures; published by Hafen Hamburg Marketing with the Hamburg Port Authority as press contact. English version at /en/press/news/cargo-handling-figures-first-to-third-quarters-of-2026/.

title: Increased Service Instability
key_claim: Weekly service instability on Asia-North Europe is 78% above its 2013-2019 baseline, and the resulting unexpected network changes create major bottlenecks at arrival ports.
frame_summary: Argues that post-pandemic service instability is structurally higher across deep-sea trades, worst on Asia-Europe, and that carrier-side network churn is a direct cause of congestion at arrival ports.
verbatim_quote: these unexpected changes create major bottlenecks at the arrival ports
verbatim_list: Asia‑North Europe seeing an massive 78% increase in weekly service instability
while Asia‑Mediterranean recorded a 71% increase.
notes: Instability measured as the standard deviation of weekly offered services, 2020-2026 against the 2013-2019 baseline.

title: Global Schedule Reliability Records a Marginal Gain in September
key_claim: Global schedule reliability was 50.6% in September 2026, up 0.9 percentage points after an aggregate 14.8-point fall from the May peak of 64.5%.
frame_summary: Presents September 2026's 50.6% as a marginal gain after three months of steep decline, framing current reliability as historically weak with delays for late vessels near record levels for the month.
verbatim_quote: Schedule reliability improved by 0.9 percentage points M/M in September 2026 to 50.6%.
verbatim_list: after three consecutive M/M drops, with an aggregate drop of ‑14.8 percentage points, from a peak of 64.5% in May.

title: Port congestion is getting worse in container shipping: who is responsible?
key_claim: Average ship waiting time nearly doubled between 2019 and 2026; a terminal at 90% berth utilisation needs about a week to recover from a one-day disruption, and capacity at nine major ports grew 21% between 2019 and 2026 while volumes grew faster.
frame_summary: Accepts that congestion is worsening but rejects a single global underinvestment story, attributing congestion to cost-optimised carrier scheduling, high terminal utilisation and a system built to optimise cost rather than resilience.
verbatim_quote: A terminal running at 90% berth utilisation takes roughly one week to recover from a one-day disruption.
verbatim_list: A terminal running at 75% utilisation can recover in two days.
terminal operators on average expanded capacity by 21% between 2019 and 2026
notes: Structural anchor at 92 days from scan date: the canonical utilisation-and-recovery arithmetic the signal's mechanism rests on.

title: Container rates to plummet in 2027
key_claim: Xeneta forecasts 2027 container demand growth of up to 4% against capacity growth of around 6.8%, with spot rates falling by as much as 30% as a full-year average.
frame_summary: Presents 2027 as a capacity-surplus year in which spot rates collapse as Red Sea routings return, while hedging that geopolitical shocks could reverse the decline.
verbatim_quote: Xeneta forecasts global container transport demand to increase by up to 4% and capacity to increase by around 6.8%
verbatim_list: collapse in spot rates by as much as 30% as a full-year average
which has already started with more than 50% of tonnage already on the shorter transits
Global container demand was up by 4.7% in the first eight months of 2026
notes: Reports Xeneta's Ocean Outlook; the strongest sourced counter-case to the signal.

title: Port delays swallow 1.7m TEU as North European congestion bites
key_claim: Vessel delays absorb around 1.7 million TEU, about 5% of deep-sea capacity against 2.2% before the pandemic, and CLECAT reports yard utilisation at Rotterdam and Antwerp regularly exceeding 90%.
frame_summary: Frames congestion as a capacity problem in which vessel delays absorb a growing share of the global fleet, with Rotterdam and Antwerp as the North European pressure points spilling onto inland transport.
verbatim_quote: Vessel delays are currently absorbing around 5% of global deep-sea container capacity, equivalent to 1.7 million TEU.
verbatim_list: Before the pandemic, delays typically tied up around 2.2% of capacity.
Yard utilisation at Rotterdam and Antwerp has regularly exceeded 90%
Global schedule reliability remains at roughly 60–65%, compared with 70–80% before the pandemic.
notes: 92 days at scan date, at the soft-window boundary; carries the CLECAT yard-utilisation figure and Sea-Intelligence delay-absorption data. Quantitative figures credited to Sea-Intelligence (19 August analysis) and CLECAT.
